title: Live Helius API key is published in public git history (including a commit message) and was never rotated
file: git history: commits bd900ed, 7ec77ec, 9237c9b, 8eb54ba (current credential in .env)
evidence: Bounded history search (values redacted to 6 chars): commit 8eb54ba (2026-08-06, initial commit) hardcodes heliusApiKey 'dfc728...' in three places; commits 9237c9b and bd900ed (2026-08-08/10) hardcode a second key 'c85473...', and bd900ed's COMMIT MESSAGE itself is 'feat: set universal Helius API key c85473...'; 7ec77ec adds UNIVERSAL_HELIUS_KEY='c85473...'. The remote is public GitHub (jgouiza-debug/pumpfun-sniper-bot), and sniperEngine.ts:345-347 confirms 'A literal used to live here and in three other places, in a public repo'. A boolean-only grep (no value printed) shows the CURRENT .env HELIUS_API_KEY matches the leaked 'c85473' prefix — the exposed key is still the live credential. The code-side removal happened (a01187e, noted in docs/research/audit-2026-08-20-phase1-full-system.md line 296) but rotation never did.
impact: Anyone who reads the public repo history can use the key: quota exhaustion and 429 storms on the exact RPC path that prices open positions and lands exits (withRpcRetry treats 429 as transient and keeps paying latency), plus billing abuse on the Helius account. The UI does surface RPC health, so it is degradation rather than a silent brick — but a stranger can throttle live exits at will, indefinitely.
proposed_fix: Rotate the Helius key in the Helius dashboard now and update .env / .api-keys.json; also revoke the older dfc728 key if it is still active. History rewriting is optional (the commit message cannot be scrubbed without a force-push rewrite) — rotation is the real fix. Add a pre-commit secret scan to keep the next key out.
verdict_reason: Facts CONFIRMED: the four commits exist; bd900ed's commit MESSAGE literally embeds the full Helius key (verified via `git log -1 --format=%s bd900ed`); initial commit 8eb54ba hardcoded the same key as a fallback in src/services/sniperEngine.ts (lines 94 and 154 of that revision — two of the 'three places'); the code-side removal is commit a01187e ('drop the embedded Helius key'); the remote is https://github.com/jgouiza-debug/pumpfun-sniper-bot.git; and a `git log --all -S<currentEnvKey>` shows the value now in .env (prefix c85473, length 36) is the SAME key present in 6 historical commits — so it was never rotated. sniperEngine.ts:345-347 corroborates 'in a public repo'. However High is not honest per the rubric: this is a Helius RPC provider credential with no signing power — it cannot spend the trading wallet or exfiltrate any private/PumpPortal key, so it cannot 'lose funds or keys.' The finding itself concedes the effect is 'degradation rather than a silent brick' and that the UI surfaces RPC health. The real impact is bounded operational: Helius quota/billing abuse and observable, trivially-rotatable RPC throttling. That is Medium (real but bounded), not a Critical funds/keys/brick nor a clearly 'major' live-path reliability hole. The leak-plus-non-rotation is a genuine, still-open hygiene problem worth fixing by rotating the key.

title: POST /api/bot/config response echoes the raw Helius and PumpPortal API keys
evidence: getConfig() (sniperEngine.ts:735-740) returns `{ ...this.config, allInSizing }` — this.config holds the resolved raw heliusApiKey and pumpPortalApiKey (sniperEngine.ts:351, 355, 483). server.ts:226 sends it verbatim: `res.json({ success: true, config: sniperEngine.getConfig() })`. This contradicts the module's own invariant — sniperEngine.ts:856-857 ('the status endpoint deliberately never returns a key') and 1273-1283 where getStatus carefully destructures both keys out and returns only set/hint fields — and the prior audit's claim (audit-2026-08-20 §5: 'Keys are stripped from getStatus so they never echo back to the UI'), which only covered getStatus. Exploit chain: GET /api/session-token (server.ts:76-78) is token-exempt (server.ts:83-86 exempts GET) and CORS-readable by ANY loopback origin on any port (apiAuth.ts:88-90, server.ts:63-66), so any page served by any localhost server can fetch the token, POST an empty body to /api/bot/config with X-Sniper-Token, and read back both keys. The code itself states the stakes: 'a funded PumpPortal key in particular can spend SOL' (sniperEngine.ts:1278-1279).
impact: Any web page served from localhost on any port (another project's dev server, Jupyter, any local tool with a compromised dependency) can exfiltrate the Helius key and the funded PumpPortal key. A stolen funded PumpPortal Lightning key spends the SOL behind it — direct fund loss; a stolen Helius key is quota theft.
proposed_fix: Make the /api/bot/config response return the same sanitized config shape getStatus builds (keys blanked, set/hint/source fields), or have getConfig() destructure privateKey/heliusApiKey/pumpPortalApiKey out exactly like sniperEngine.ts:1282 does. copyTraderService.ts:551 (the only internal consumer needing the raw key) can use a dedicated internal accessor.
verdict_reason: Fully verified in the working tree. getConfig() (sniperEngine.ts:736-739) returns `{ ...this.config, allInSizing }`, and this.config carries the resolved raw heliusApiKey and pumpPortalApiKey (351, 355, 483). server.ts:224-226 echoes getConfig() verbatim in the POST /api/bot/config response. This genuinely violates the module's own stated invariant: getStatus (1282) destructures BOTH keys out and returns only a set/last-4 hint (1273-1283). Exploit chain holds against the code read: GET /api/session-token is exempt from the token (server.ts:83-86 returns next() for GET/HEAD/OPTIONS) and CORS reflects any loopback Origin (server.ts:63-66 with apiAuth.ts:83-93 accepting localhost/127.0.0.1/::1 on ANY port), so a page served from any localhost port reads the token; it can then send X-Sniper-Token (allowed header, server.ts:65) on a POST whose CORS preflight passes for the loopback origin, and read back both raw keys — including the funded PumpPortal key the code itself notes 'can spend SOL' (1278-1279). Severity High is honest: it can leak a fund-spending key, but requires an attacker foothold already serving a page from a loopback origin (evil.com is blocked by originGuard, apiAuth.ts:100-108), so it is defence-in-depth rather than a direct funds-loss path — High, not Critical.

title: API bearer token is handed to any loopback-origin page via GET /api/session-token
evidence: GET /api/session-token returns apiToken() (server.ts:76-78). The token gate exempts all GETs (server.ts:83-86), originGuard allows every loopback origin on every port (apiAuth.ts:88-90, comment at 22-25: 'Loopback origins stay allowed on every port'), and the cors() middleware reflects those origins so the response is readable cross-port (server.ts:63-66). The design rationale (instance switcher, vite on :3010) is documented, and apiAuth.ts:27-30 honestly scopes the token against 'a local process running as this user' — but a page served from localhost is a wider class than a local process: it includes any third-party JS running in any locally hosted web app.
impact: Any localhost-served page gains the full mutating surface: sell/close positions, rewrite strategy config, toggle real trading, add copy-trade leaders, link/unlink the wallet (including deleting .photon-wallet.json), trigger the self-updater — and, via the config echo (separate finding), read both API keys. The bearer token's defence-in-depth is void inside the loopback-origin class it was partly meant to gate.
proposed_fix: Stop serving the token to arbitrary loopback origins: restrict /api/session-token to same-port requests (check Host/Referer or drop the endpoint and rely solely on the token injected into the served index.html, server.ts:114-120), and have the instance switcher pass the token explicitly (operator pastes it once per target instance).
verdict_reason: Verified: GET /api/session-token returns apiToken() (server.ts:76-78); the /api token middleware exempts GET/HEAD/OPTIONS (server.ts:83-86); originGuard passes every loopback origin (apiAuth.ts:100-108 with isLoopbackOrigin 83-93) and cors() reflects those origins so the JSON body is cross-port readable (server.ts:63-66). Because mutating endpoints DO require the token (requireApiToken, apiAuth.ts:128-136), a page served from any localhost port can GET the token then POST to the full mutating surface (sell, real-mode toggle, add copy leaders, wallet unlink/delete, updater). The in-code rationale (server.ts:71-78: 'exposes nothing a same-machine browser page could not already reach') is refuted by the token gate it sits in front of — a loopback page could NOT already reach those endpoints without the token. Medium is honest: severe fund-affecting surface, but gated behind the precondition of attacker-controlled JS on a loopback origin. No missed guard refutes it.

title: .photon-wallet.json is read/written at process.cwd(), not the packaged-exe base dir every other secret file uses
evidence: WALLET_FILE = path.resolve(process.cwd(), '.photon-wallet.json') (walletService.ts:26), used by autoLoad (186-194), link persist (321-327) and unlink delete (345-348). Every other per-install secret follows the packaged rule `isPackaged ? path.dirname(process.execPath) : process.cwd()`: keyStore.ts:44-47, apiAuth.ts:36-39, loadEnv.ts:29-30, fileLogger.ts:21-22. keyStore.ts:20-23 even claims .photon-wallet.json already follows 'the same base-directory rule' — it does not. fileLogger.ts:6-7 names the concrete case: 'a Task Scheduler launch has cwd C:\Windows\System32'.
impact: A packaged exe launched with cwd != exe dir (Task Scheduler, a shortcut with a different Start-in, a shell in another directory) writes the plaintext Solana signing key into that unrelated directory — outside the install dir and outside the .gitignore'd project — and on the next normal launch silently fails to auto-load the persisted wallet (looks like the wallet vanished). Stray plaintext key copies accumulate in unpredictable locations.
proposed_fix: Compute WALLET_FILE with the same isPackaged/execPath rule as keyStore.keyStorePath(); on startup, migrate an existing cwd-located file to the base dir. Apply the same to .copy-trader.json (copyTraderService.ts:64) for consistency, though it holds no secrets.
verdict_reason: Verified: WALLET_FILE = path.resolve(process.cwd(), '.photon-wallet.json') at walletService.ts:26 with no isPackaged branch, used by autoLoad (186-194), link persist (321-327) and unlink delete (345-348). Every other per-install secret uses the packaged base-dir rule: keyStore.ts:44-47, apiAuth.ts:36-39, loadEnv.ts:29-30, fileLogger.ts:21-22. fileLogger.ts:6-7 names the concrete cwd=C:\Windows\System32 Task Scheduler case. So a packaged exe launched with cwd != exe dir writes the plaintext signing key to an unrelated, non-gitignored directory and fails to auto-load it on a normal launch. Minor imprecision in the finding's prose (keyStore.ts:20-24 literally attaches 'same base-directory rule' to .api-token/.env, and loosely lumps .photon-wallet.json under 'same treatment') does not affect the substantive divergence, which is real. Medium fits: bounded key-hygiene + reliability impact, visible (not a silent brick), no direct adversarial fund loss.

title: bot.log (console tee of all runtime output) is not gitignored in a public repo
evidence: fileLogger.ts:22 writes bot.log (and rotation file bot.log.1, line 37) to cwd in dev — the repo root. `git check-ignore bot.log` returns non-zero (not ignored) and `git status --porcelain` shows it untracked ('?? bot.log'); .gitignore covers reports/, flags.json and all secret files but not bot.log. The current file contains no key material (0 hits for 'api-key='), and the tee'd console lines were verified to print only hosts, key paths and last-4 hints — but it does record wallet addresses, balances and full trade activity.
impact: One `git add .` or `git add -A` (the working tree already mixes docs and code changes for bulk commits, e.g. commit fbac394 'Include repository config and docs' swept in Run_As_Admin.cmd) publishes operational logs — wallet address, balances, trade timing — to the public repo. If any future log line ever includes an error carrying a URL or key, it ships too.
proposed_fix: Add `bot.log` and `bot.log.*` to .gitignore.
verdict_reason: Verified: fileLogger.ts:22 writes bot.log (rotation .1 at line 37) to cwd in dev = repo root. Read the full .gitignore (30 lines) — it covers .photon-wallet.json, .env, .api-token, .api-keys.json, flags.json, reports/, dist-exe/ but NOT bot.log. `git check-ignore bot.log` returns exit 1 (not ignored) and `git status --porcelain` shows `?? bot.log`; the file exists (1433 bytes). A bulk `git add -A` would publish it. Low is honest: the log records wallet address/balances/trade timing (real leak surface) but the tee formats args and no key material is present today; impact requires an accidental bulk commit.

title: Dead private-key parser getKeypairFromPrivateKey duplicates WalletService.parseSecret
evidence: getKeypairFromPrivateKey (sniperEngine.ts:1402-1427) has zero call sites anywhere in src/ (grep confirms only the definition). It is a second, divergent key-parsing implementation alongside WalletService.parseSecret (walletService.ts:204-270), which carries the hard-won base58-before-base64 ordering fix and its rationale (walletService.ts:244-251).
impact: A future caller reaching for the nearest parser gets the unmaintained copy, forking key-format behavior from the wallet-link path. Bounded: currently unreachable code, no runtime exposure.
proposed_fix: Delete the method; route any future need through WalletService.parseSecret.
verdict_reason: Verified: getKeypairFromPrivateKey is a private method at sniperEngine.ts:1402-1427; grep across src/ returns only the definition line — zero call sites. As a private member it is reachable only within sniperEngine.ts, and it is never invoked, so it is dead code. It is a divergent parser vs WalletService.parseSecret (walletService.ts:204-270): it has no base64 branch, no 64-hex seed branch, no comma-separated branch, and does bs58.decode without the documented base58-before-base64 rationale (walletService.ts:244-256). Low is honest — unreachable today, no runtime exposure; the risk is a future caller adopting the unmaintained copy.

title: Release and exe builds still execute dependency install scripts (phaseB #9 fix not implemented)
evidence: Both install steps in C:\Users\Rever\Documents\New folder\.github\workflows\release.yml (line 45 and line 114) run plain `npm ci` with no `--ignore-scripts`, and the local `build:exe` script (package.json line 9) builds from a normally-installed node_modules. phaseB-2026-08-21-red-team.md lines 208-210 explicitly prescribed "`npm ci --ignore-scripts` in CI and release builds" as the fix for attack 9 (dependency exfiltrates the keypair). Current install-script surface measured from the lockfile/hasInstallScript and node_modules scan: bufferutil@4.1.0 (install: node-gyp-build, prod optional), utf-8-validate@6.0.6 (install: node-gyp-build, prod optional), esbuild@0.25.12 (postinstall: node install.js, dev), fsevents@2.3.3 (dev optional, mac-only) — identical to phaseB's measurement, all canonical.
impact: If any transitive dep ships a malicious install hook after the owner next refreshes the lockfile (`npm update`/re-resolve), the script executes on the machine that produces the distributed exe and that also runs the live bot — this working tree's dist-exe/ holds live state (.api-keys.json, .api-token, .copy-trader.json, bot.log) and the user profile holds .env with HELIUS_API_KEY, all reachable by an install script. The Aug 4 2026 keyv/cacheable worm (2,234 poisoned versions, 444 packages) is exactly this vector; this repo's lockfile has zero keyv/cacheable packages today, but the control is absent, not the threat.
proposed_fix: Add `--ignore-scripts` to both `npm ci` invocations in release.yml and use it for local exe builds. Verified feasible: bufferutil/utf-8-validate are optional ws perf addons (ws falls back to JS), and esbuild works from its platform package @esbuild/win32-x64 without its postinstall check. Keep `npm ci` (lockfile-validating) as-is otherwise.
verdict_reason: Verified: release.yml runs `npm i -g npm@11` then bare `npm ci` at line 45 (windows job) and line 114 (macos job), neither with --ignore-scripts; build:exe (package.json:9) builds from a normally-installed node_modules. Install scripts do run (esbuild postinstall, node-gyp-build for bufferutil/utf-8-validate), so the missing control is not moot. Two real blast radii: the CI runner produces the distributed exe every client auto-updates to, and the local build:exe machine holds .env/HELIUS_API_KEY and runs the live bot. phaseB #9 prescribed exactly `npm ci --ignore-scripts`; still not implemented (still_open). Medium is defensible: real but bounded preventive-control gap, requires a future malicious dep after a lockfile refresh; not Critical (no current exploitable dep), not Low (blast radius is the shipped binary + key-holding machine).

title: uuid 8.3.2 (GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq) on the runtime RPC path via @solana/web3.js -> jayson
evidence: npm audit: uuid <11.1.1, moderate, GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq (missing buffer bounds check in v3/v5/v6 when a buf is provided; CWE-787). Resolution chain confirmed via npm ls: @solana/web3.js@1.98.4 -> jayson@4.3.0 -> uuid@8.3.2 (package-lock.json line 4289), production runtime path (jayson is web3.js's JSON-RPC client). jayson declares uuid ^8.3.2 (node_modules/jayson/package.json line 61) and uses v4 request IDs, not v3/v5/v6-with-buf. npm's only offered fix is downgrading @solana/web3.js to 0.0.3 (isSemVerMajor). Also flagged: jayson >=2.0.6 and @solana/web3.js <=1.98.4 as moderate, both purely transitive echoes of this same uuid advisory.
impact: None reachable in this codebase: the vulnerable functions (uuid.v3/v5/v6 with an attacker-influenced undersized buffer) are never invoked on this path; jayson generates v4 ids internally. The real hazard is operational: running `npm audit fix --force` would downgrade @solana/web3.js to 0.0.3 and brick every trade path.
proposed_fix: Accept and monitor until @solana/web3.js ships with a jayson that bumps uuid; do NOT run `npm audit fix --force` (prior audit made the same call, audit-2026-08-20-phase1-full-system.md lines 300-304). Optionally add an npm `overrides` entry for jayson>uuid only after verifying jayson's require('uuid').v4 usage against uuid 9/11 exports.
verdict_reason: Verified: uuid pinned to 8.3.2 (package-lock.json:4289-4298). Chain confirmed: @solana/web3.js depends on jayson ^4.1.1 (web3.js/package.json:70), jayson resolved to 4.3.0 depends on uuid ^8.3.2 (jayson/package.json:61), production JSON-RPC path. GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq affects uuid v3/v5/v6 only when a buffer is provided; jayson imports only `require('uuid').v4` and calls it with no buffer (utils.js:6, generateRequest.js:3, client/browser/index.js:3), so the vulnerable code is unreachable. The finding rates it Low, states 'None reachable,' and correctly flags the operational trap that `npm audit fix --force` would downgrade web3.js to 0.0.3. Honest and accurate; Low stands.

title: nanoid 3.3.17 high advisory (GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8) in build toolchain — devDeps only, trivially updatable
evidence: npm audit: nanoid <3.3.18, rated high, GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8 (custom generators can loop indefinitely when size is zero, CWE-835). npm ls confirms the only path is vite@6.4.3 -> postcss@8.5.25 -> nanoid@3.3.17 (package-lock.json line 3465), devDependencies, build-time only — never in the shipped exe or the running server. The vulnerable code path (customAlphabet/customRandom with size 0) is not something postcss invokes. Prior audits ran `npm audit --omit=dev` (phaseA-2026-08-20-self-verification.md line 112) so this never appeared before; it is new visibility, not a regression.
impact: Worst case is a hung `vite build` on the dev machine — no live-trading exposure. Left unfixed it is audit noise that could train the owner to ignore a future genuine high.
proposed_fix: `npm update nanoid` — 3.3.18+ satisfies postcss's ^3.3.11 range; lockfile-only change, no code impact.
verdict_reason: package-lock.json node_modules/nanoid resolves to 3.3.17, matching the <3.3.18 advisory (GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8). Its only path is via vite (package.json:59, devDependencies) -> postcss -> nanoid, all build/dev-time; production dependencies (package.json:36-47: web3.js/express/ws/axios) do not pull nanoid. Worst case is a hung vite build on the dev machine, no live-trading exposure. Low is honest.

title: pkg config and comment claim the shipped exe is Node 18; the actual build uses `--targets host` (exe embeds Node 24.18.1) and the documented bare-`pkg .` fallback would ship an EOL runtime
evidence: package.json line 31-33 pins pkg targets to ["node18-win-x64"], and the //targets comment (line 30) states "Windows stays on node18 (its prebuilt base exists and the shipped exe is built from it)". But build:exe (line 9) passes `--targets host`, which overrides that field. Binary inspection of dist-exe/pumpfun-sniper-bot.exe (185 MB, built Aug 24): version-string scan finds v24.18.1 and zero occurrences of any 18.20.x string — the shipped exe embeds Node 24.18.1 (host machine runs v24.16.0; @yao-pkg/pkg fetched the latest v24 base). Node 18 reached end-of-life 2025-04-30.
impact: The shipped Windows exe is fine (Node 24 is in support). The risk is the documented fallback: the comment explicitly endorses "a bare `pkg .`" as a valid way to build the Windows exe, and that path would embed EOL Node 18.20.x — no OpenSSL/undici/http security patches — into a binary distributed to other people, while the config comment tells the builder this is expected. Doc-vs-reality drift in a security-relevant build setting.
proposed_fix: Change pkg.targets to ["node22-win-x64"] (matching the mac builds) or ["node24-win-x64"], and rewrite the //targets comment to state that build:exe uses `--targets host` and what runtime the shipped exe actually embeds.
verdict_reason: package.json:9 build:exe uses `--targets host`, overriding the pkg.targets ['node18-win-x64'] field (line 32), and the //targets comment (line 30) explicitly endorses a bare `pkg .` as a valid Windows build path. Binary scan of dist-exe/pumpfun-sniper-bot.exe: 14 occurrences of v24.18.1 and zero v18.x strings, so the shipped exe embeds Node 24 (in-support) but the documented fallback would ship EOL Node 18. Doc-vs-reality drift verified end-to-end. Low is honest.

title: Signed transactions from PumpPortal trade-local are never verified against intent before signing/broadcast
evidence: On the live path the bot POSTs to https://pumpportal.fun/api/trade-local (sniperEngine.ts:1535), deserializes the returned bytes (`tx = VersionedTransaction.deserialize(remoteTxBytes)`, line 1562), then `tx.sign([keypair])` (line 1566) and `sendRawTransaction(tx.serialize(), { skipPreflight: true })` (line 1569). Nothing between deserialize and sign inspects the message: no check that the fee payer is our wallet, that instructions target only the pump program / expected mint, that lamport/token amounts match `solAmount`/`maxSolCost`, or that no extra SystemProgram transfer / token approve to a third party is present. `skipPreflight: true` also removes the simulate step that could catch an anomalous tx. The only structural check, localTxBuilder.shadowCompare (localTxBuilder.ts:249), runs fire-and-forget AFTER submission and only when the localTxShadowCompare flag is on (sniperEngine.ts:1580) — it never gates the signature. verifySellPath (sniperEngine.ts:3573) also signs whatever trade-local returns.
impact: A malicious or compromised PumpPortal response (or any successful MITM of that HTTPS hop) returns a transaction whose instructions the wallet keypair blindly signs and broadcasts — e.g. a System transfer of the whole wallet balance to an attacker, or a token-account authority change. Because the same wallet builds 100% of buys and sells this way, a single hostile response can drain the linked wallet. The machinery to verify intent (compare accounts/discriminator/data against a locally built tx) already exists in localTxBuilder but is only used for post-hoc shadow logging, not as a pre-sign gate.
proposed_fix: Before tx.sign, assert the decoded VersionedTransaction: fee payer == our pubkey; every writable-signed account is ours; the pump-program instruction targets `mint`; the buy amount/maxSolCost (or sell percentage) match the requested intent; and reject any unexpected SystemProgram transfer or Token approve/setAuthority instruction. Reuse localTxBuilder.describe()/shadowCompare logic synchronously to fail closed when the returned tx does not match intent.
verdict_reason: Primary claim verified: on the live path executeRealMainnetTrade POSTs to pumpportal.fun/api/trade-local (1535), does `tx = VersionedTransaction.deserialize(remoteTxBytes)` (1562), then immediately `tx.sign([keypair])` (1566) and `sendRawTransaction(tx.serialize(), { skipPreflight: true })` (1569-1572), with nothing between deserialize and sign checking fee payer, program IDs, target mint, or amounts, and skipPreflight removing the simulate step. The only structural check, localTxBuilder.shadowCompare (localTxBuilder.ts:249-302), runs fire-and-forget AFTER submission (1580-1587), only for buys, only when the localTxShadowCompare flag is on, and merely logs — it never gates the signature. So a compromised/malicious trade-local response (or TLS MITM of that hop) would be blindly signed and broadcast, and because the same wallet builds every buy and sell this way, a single hostile response could drain the wallet (unbounded, not Medium's 'bounded' impact). One secondary claim is INACCURATE and does not hold: verifySellPath (3563-3591) does NOT sign — it passes the deserialized tx to simulateSellPath, which calls connection.simulateTransaction with sigVerify:false (honeypotDetector.ts:218), never signing or broadcasting, so that path cannot lose funds. This error does not change the confirmed live-execution exposure. Severity stays High rather than Critical because the impact requires an external precondition — compromise of pumpportal.fun or a TLS MITM — not a code bug or the bot's routine adversaries; the whole architecture already delegates 100% of tx construction to that trusted service.

title: Copy-trade BUY slippage can reach 100%, bypassing the 30% buy ceiling the engine enforces on its own orders
evidence: sanitizeConfig clamps the copy trader's maxSlippagePct to [1,100] (copyTraderService.ts:2182). That value is handed to sniperEngine.executeExternalTrade('buy', ..., this.config.maxSlippagePct) (copyTraderService.ts:1383), which forwards it as `slippageOverride` into executeRealMainnetTrade. There the buy slippage is computed as `effectiveSlippage = Math.max(1, Math.min(100, slippageOverride ?? baseSlippage))` (sniperEngine.ts:1456) — when an override is present the engine's own `configured` value is ignored. The sniper's OWN config path caps buy slippage at 30 via clampConfig (`['maxSlippagePct', 1, 30]`, sniperEngine.ts:802, with the comment 'Ceiling of 30, not 100 ... consent to be sandwiched'), but copy config is never run through clampConfig. So the identical executeRealMainnetTrade buy that is limited to 30% for the sniper is limited only to 100% for a copy trade.
impact: An operator who raises copy 'Max Slippage' (UI field, CopyTradingPage.tsx:666; default 25) up to 100 makes copy buys fill at up to 2x the quoted price — the exact overpay/sandwich exposure the engine deliberately forbids on its own buys. maxSolCost in the built tx scales with (1+slippage), so a copy buy can commit far more SOL than the nominal size.
proposed_fix: Clamp the copy buy slippage to the same buy ceiling the engine uses (30), e.g. cap sanitizeConfig.maxSlippagePct at 30 or split copy buy/sell slippage so the buy override passed at copyTraderService.ts:1383 cannot exceed 30 while sells stay wider.
verdict_reason: Verified the full chain: copyTraderService.ts:2182 clamps copy maxSlippagePct to [1,100]; :1383 passes it as the slippageOverride arg to executeExternalTrade; sniperEngine.ts:4050 forwards it unchanged to executeRealMainnetTrade; :1456 computes effectiveSlippage = Math.max(1, Math.min(100, slippageOverride ?? baseSlippage)), so an override ignores the engine's own 30-capped `configured`. The sniper's clampConfig caps its OWN maxSlippagePct at 30 (:802, with the 'consent to be sandwiched' comment) but copy config never passes through clampConfig — its only clamp is sanitizeConfig at 100. UI default is 25 (CopyTradingPage.tsx:666) but the ceiling is 100. effectiveSlippage feeds the PumpPortal build slippage (:1543). Real overpay/sandwich exposure on the live buy path; Medium is honest.

title: No runtime RPC failover — the Connection is resolved once and never fails over on a dead credential or outage

title: Failed manual LIQUIDATE silently marks a REAL position CLOSED and zeroes tokensHeld, orphaning tokens still in the wallet
evidence: NEW uncommitted code in runExit (copyTraderService.ts:1662-1695). For a real position, when executeRealSell returns null it now runs, if isManual: `pos.status='CLOSED'; pos.tokensHeld=0;` and pushes a history record `exitReason: 'Manual liquidation (closed after external exit)'`. But executeRealSell (copyTraderService.ts:1795-1852) returns null after COPY_SELL_MAX_ATTEMPTS on-chain FAILURES (slippage 6004, on-chain reject, or a timeout resolved as failed/expired via resolveTimedOutSell) — in every one of those the tokens were NOT sold and remain in the wallet. It also returns null if the operator flips to paper mid-retry (line 1824). The code assumes null means 'tokens already gone externally', but null overwhelmingly means 'the sell failed and the bag is still held'. The manual path is reached from manualSellPosition->closePosition with via:'manual' (line 442-453), i.e. the operator pressed LIQUIDATE expecting a sell.
impact: Operator presses LIQUIDATE on a real copy position. The venue is temporarily illiquid / RPC is storming / slippage is tight, so all 6 attempts fail. Instead of keeping the position for retry (old behavior), the bot marks it CLOSED, zeroes tokensHeld, drops it from persistence (persist() filters status!=='CLOSED', line 2048), stops all price/exit watching, and books a fake sell reading 'closed after external exit'. The real tokens sit unattended in the wallet and can ride to zero while the operator believes the position was liquidated. Reintroduces the exact stranded-bag failure the rest of the file guards against.
proposed_fix: Do not treat a failed executeRealSell as a successful close. Only auto-close after confirming the wallet's on-chain token balance for pos.mint is ~0 (e.g. read the token account, or require inspectFill evidence of zero holdings). Otherwise keep the position OPEN and surface the failure (as before), and keep the true 'dismiss already-liquidated' action separate and explicit (forceClosePosition).
verdict_reason: Verified in working tree. runExit (copyTraderService.ts:1662-1695) sets pos.status='CLOSED', pos.tokensHeld=0, calls unsubscribeMintIfIdle, and books a 'Manual liquidation (closed after external exit)' history record whenever executeRealSell returns null on the manual path. executeRealSell (1795-1852) returns null after COPY_SELL_MAX_ATTEMPTS on-chain failures (1851) or a mid-retry flip to paper mode (1824); in every one of those the tokens were NOT sold and remain in the wallet. The line-1814 null (manual-takeover) is guarded by !isManual and is unreachable on the manual path, so it does not weaken the finding. The manual SELL button routes manualSellPosition->closePosition(fraction=1, via:'manual') (442-452), i.e. the operator expected a sell. Note executeRealSell first pushes a 'position kept' feed message (1848-1849) that runExit then contradicts by closing the position — misleading as well as harmful. High is honest: this is a missed exit that orphans a real bag; not Critical because in the common illiquid/rug case the tokens are already worthless and the operator does receive a 'failed' feed message at the time.

title: Unsigned-PumpPortal dedup keys off the GLOBAL isHealthy() and is never checked by the fast/normal Helius paths, allowing duplicate real buys/sells
evidence: handlePumpPortalMessage: when a PumpPortal payload carries no signature it decides whether to execute solely from `if (this.logWatcher?.isHealthy() ?? false) return;` (line 1111), otherwise executes and records unsignedCopies[mint:side] (1112). isHealthy() (walletLogWatcher.ts:143-149) returns false if ANY tracked sub is unacked — it loops ALL subs. On add-wallet (setAddresses, walletLogWatcher.ts:123-136) existing subs stay live and keep DELIVERING while the new sub is unacked, so isHealthy() is false even though the trading leader's own subscription is live. The unsignedCopies guard is only consulted on the 20s retry path (`if (isRetry)`, copyTraderService.ts:712-722); handleFastLog (738-790) and the normal handleWalletLog dispatch (724) never check it.
impact: During any window where a tracked leader's sub is live but another wallet's sub is momentarily unacked (add-wallet, multi-wallet startup ack ramp), an unsigned PumpPortal buy/sell for that leader is executed as 'sole source', and Helius then ALSO delivers the same tx (pump.fun via the fast lane, which has no unsignedCopies check) and executes it again. Result: a duplicated real BUY (folds in as a DCA add, doubling intended size when blockRepeatBuys is off) or a duplicated real SELL (oversell). Cross-lane signature dedup can't catch it because the PumpPortal leg had no signature.
proposed_fix: Gate the unsigned fallback on a PER-LEADER liveness check (is THIS address's subscription acked), not global isHealthy(); and consult unsignedCopies in handleFastLog and the normal handleWalletLog dispatch, not only the isRetry branch, so a Helius delivery of an already-unsigned-copied trade is dropped regardless of path.
verdict_reason: Verified. handlePumpPortalMessage decides to execute an unsigned payload solely from `if (this.logWatcher?.isHealthy() ?? false) return;` (copyTraderService.ts:1111) and records unsignedCopies[mint:side] (1112). isHealthy() (walletLogWatcher.ts:143-149) returns false if ANY sub has subId===undefined; setAddresses (123-136) leaves existing acked subs untouched (they keep subId and keep delivering) while a newly added sub is unacked, so during add-wallet/startup ack-ramp isHealthy() is false even though the tracked leader's own Helius sub is live and WILL deliver the same tx. The unsignedCopies guard is consulted ONLY on the isRetry branch (712-722); handleFastLog (738-790, marks sig processed at 781 then dispatches at 786-788 with no unsignedCopies check) and the first-read analysis dispatch (724) never check it. Cross-lane processedSigs dedup cannot fire because the PumpPortal leg carried no signature. Result: the leader's trade executes once from PumpPortal (sole source) and again from Helius. For a buy, blockRepeatBuys defaults false (188) and 1242/1305 let the second buy fold into the existing position as a DCA add via the per-mint tradeQueue, doubling size (each leg clamped to maxBuySol at 1278); for a sell it oversells (the code's own comment at 1108 notes '75% out'). Matches High (duplicated buys / wrong trades). Recurs on every multi-wallet add and startup ack ramp, so not a mere theoretical race; not Critical because size is bounded by maxBuySol/holdings and a sell cannot exceed wallet balance.

title: leaderBalances tally is written by concurrent async paths with no ordering guard; a late reconcile clobbers a newer balance and mis-sizes the next mirror sell
evidence: handleFastLog updates the tally synchronously with exact TradeEvent amounts (line 779), then fires `void this.reconcileLeaderBalances(...)` (785) which fetches the tx ~1s later and unconditionally overwrites via recordLeaderBalances -> `this.leaderBalances.set(...)` (814). analyzeLeaderTx also writes it unconditionally (898). There is no slot/version/ordering guard: reconciles for different txs of the same mint can complete out of order relative to the newer synchronous fast-lane updates, so an OLDER tx's post-balance can overwrite a NEWER one. reconcileLeaderBalances is additionally skipped entirely when txFetchQueue.length>4 (793), so under congestion the correction is dropped.
impact: For a leader spamming sub-second same-mint trades, the tally can transiently hold a stale (usually too-high) balance. A fast-lane SELL sized during that window computes leaderSellFraction = sold/tally against the wrong denominator (copyTraderService.ts:761-763, copyExitPolicy leaderSellFraction), producing a mirror sell of the wrong percentage (under- or over-sell). Self-corrects on the next reconcile, so impact is transient, but it is a wrong-size real order.
proposed_fix: Guard leaderBalances writes with the tx slot/ordering (only apply a reconcile whose slot is >= the last applied for that address:mint), or skip reconcile entirely for txs the exact-amount fast lane already accounted for. At minimum, do not let a fetched reconcile overwrite a value updated by a strictly-later event.
verdict_reason: leaderBalances is written by three unsynchronized paths: fast-lane synchronous tally (copyTraderService.ts:779), reconcileLeaderBalances -> recordLeaderBalances (:814), and analyzeLeaderTx (:898). recordLeaderBalances (:800-815) sets each mint unconditionally with no slot/version/ordering guard, and reconcileLeaderBalances is dropped entirely when txFetchQueue.length>4 (:793). Since reconciles are fire-and-forget (:785) and complete out of order, an older tx's post-balance can overwrite a newer synchronous update. The sell fraction is sold/tracked via leaderSellFraction (copyExitPolicy.ts:41-46) using sig.remainingTokens captured at :762 from the tally, consumed at :1548 for a real mirror sell. The guard at :761 (tracked < tokens -> defer to analysis path) only protects the over-sell direction, leaving the finding's stale-high -> under-sell case live. Self-corrects on next reconcile, and the src/tests are sequential so they cannot exercise the interleaving. Transient wrong-size real order; Medium is honest.

title: Sniper sizing does not subtract the copy trader's in-flight buy reservations (shared wallet), risking joint overdraft
evidence: The copy trader correctly subtracts the sniper's in-flight entries when sizing (copyTraderService.ts:1353 uses sniperEngine.getInFlightEntryReservedSol()). The reverse is missing: sniper sizing computes `reservedByPeers = (this.entriesInFlight.size-1) * reservedPerEntrySol()` (sniperEngine.ts:2774) and deploys `wallet.getDeployableSol() - reservedByPeers` (2775) — it counts only its OWN in-flight entries and never subtracts copyTrader.inFlightBuySol, which claims real SOL on the same signer.
impact: If both engines are armed in real mode and buy different mints concurrently, the sniper sizes against a balance that still shows the copy trader's in-flight SOL as free, so its order can overdraft — a failed on-chain buy (burned priority fee) or an eaten copy-exit-gas reserve. The copy trader keeps working when the sniper is idle by design, but nothing prevents both being armed.
proposed_fix: Expose the copy trader's total in-flight reserved SOL and subtract it in the sniper's deployable calculation (mirror of what the copy side already does), so both engines size against a common view of committed-but-unspent SOL.
verdict_reason: Verified at sniperEngine.ts:2772-2775: in real mode the sniper sets availableTradeSol = getDeployableSol() - reservedByPeers, where reservedByPeers counts only (entriesInFlight.size-1)*reservedPerEntrySol — its OWN in-flight entries. Grep of sniperEngine.ts shows zero references to copyTrader or inFlightBuySol, so the copy trader's in-flight buy SOL on the same signer is never subtracted. The reverse guard exists and is deliberate: copyTraderService.ts:1353 subtracts sniperEngine.getInFlightEntryReservedSol(). The asymmetry is real; both engines can be armed in real mode with nothing preventing it. Impact (overdraft -> burned priority fee, or an eaten copy-exit-gas reserve that can cascade into a missed exit) is bounded but touches the live path. Medium is honest.

title: One-position-per-mint: a second tracked leader's sell mirrors against a position opened by a different leader
evidence: Positions are keyed by mint only. onLeaderBuy/recordBuy fold any repeat buy of a held mint into the single existing position regardless of which leader triggered it (copyTraderService.ts:1241, 1452 DCA merge). onLeaderSell finds the position purely by `p.mint === sig.mint` with no leader match (1536). So if leaders A and B are both tracked and both trade mint X, they share one position, and B selling triggers a mirror exit of the shared bag (sized from B's fraction).
impact: A sell by leader B closes/partially-exits a position whose thesis was leader A, and the mirror fraction is computed from B's bag, not the shared position — muddled sizing and an unintended exit when two tracked leaders overlap on a memecoin. Bounded and arguably a consequence of the copy-ALL design, but surprising with real money.
proposed_fix: Either key positions by (leader, mint) so each leader's copy is independent, or explicitly document/limit that overlapping leaders share one mint position and choose a deterministic owner/sizing rule.
verdict_reason: Verified: positions are keyed by mint only. Buy path resolves existing with this.positions.find(p => p.mint === mint ...) (copyTraderService.ts:1241) and recordBuy DCA-merges any repeat buy of a held mint into the single existing position (1452-1464) with no leader match. onLeaderSell finds the position purely by p.mint === sig.mint (1536, and again inside the queue at 1586), with the mirror fraction taken from the selling leader's own bag via leaderSellFraction(sig.tokenAmount, sig.remainingTokens) (1548) applied to the shared pos. So two tracked leaders overlapping on one mint share a position and leader B's sell partially exits a bag that A also funded, sized from B's fraction. No guard refutes this. Severity Low is honest: bounded, requires two tracked leaders on the same memecoin, and follows from the copy-ALL design.

title: leaderBalances map grows unbounded (never pruned except on reconnect/drop)
evidence: leaderBalances is keyed `address:mint` and written in handleFastLog (779) and recordLeaderBalances (814), including zero entries for closed accounts (812). It is only cleared wholesale on a watcher reconnect (619) or dropped per-leader on a retry-drop (695-697); individual keys are never pruned, and zero-balance entries are retained.

It is cleared wholesale only on a watcher reconnect (619) and dropped per-leader only on a retry-drop (695-697); individual keys are never pruned and zeros never evicted. title: Migration entries act on a fabricated liquidity constant with no on-chain pool verification
evidence: processIncomingToken, for a migrate event whose DexScreener pool has not indexed, sets launchData.liquidityUsd = 2*79*solPrice and launchData.liquidityIsAsserted=true (sniperEngine.ts:2061-2067). The comment at 2060 says 'Everything that treats liquidity as evidence must consult liquidityIsAsserted first', but the flag is only written to the latency timeline (2068) and is never read again (grep: liquidityIsAsserted appears only at 2060/2065/2068). routePlay then applies the Play 3 liquidity floor to that asserted number blind — playbookRouter.ts:270-273 checks input.liquidityUsd < config.minLiquiditySol*solPrice with no asserted-ness check. Nothing on the entry path does a getAccountInfo on the pump-amm pool to confirm it exists, is owned by the AMM, or holds reserves: localTxBuilder refuses migrated tokens (localTxBuilder.ts:170), and executeRealMainnetTrade routes trade-local with pool=payload.pool (sniperEngine.ts:1554). The entire migration decision rests on one 'txType'/'pool' string from the PumpPortal websocket.
impact: A spoofed migration event, or a real graduation whose LP the deployer pulls in the next slot, passes the Play 3 liquidity floor on the ~$12.5k asserted constant and the bot buys. Because the pool depth was never read on-chain, the bot cannot know it is buying into an empty or already-drained pool; combined with finding #2 the position then has no working drain exit either.
proposed_fix: Before committing a migration buy, do one getAccountInfo on the destination pool: confirm the account exists, is owned by the pump-amm program, and decode real SOL/token reserves. Feed those reserves (not the 2*79 assertion) to the router floor, and refuse the entry when the pool is unverifiable. At minimum, make routePlay / commitEntry refuse when launchData.liquidityIsAsserted is true and the play's floor would only pass on the asserted value.
verdict_reason: Verified end to end. For a migration whose DexScreener pool is unindexed, sniperEngine.ts:2061-2067 writes launchData.liquidityUsd = 2*79*solPriceUsd and launchData.liquidityIsAsserted=true. grep confirms liquidityIsAsserted is consumed only in offline research (research/labelOutcomes.ts:61,109) and the diagnostic latencyTimeline (2068) — it is NEVER read on the entry/routing path, so the safety flag the comment at 2059-2060 demands ('everything that treats liquidity as evidence must consult liquidityIsAsserted first') is dead code. The asserted value flows launchData.liquidityUsd -> filterResult.liquidityUsd (2430) -> routePlay input.liquidityUsd (2709), and the Play 3 floor (playbookRouter.ts:270-273) compares it to minLiquiditySol*solPrice with no asserted-ness gate, so the ~$12.5k-25k constant clears the floor blind. No getAccountInfo/getMultipleAccounts exists in sniperEngine.ts; localTxBuilder refuses migrated tokens (localTxBuilder.ts:170), so the real buy goes to PumpPortal trade-local with pool: pool||'auto' (1554) using launchData?.pool (2905) under skipPreflight:true (1570) — no on-chain confirmation the pump-amm pool exists, is AMM-owned, or holds reserves. A real graduation whose LP is pulled, or a spoofed migrate/pool string, passes the floor on the fabricated number and the bot buys. High is honest: it is a major reliability hole in the live entry path where the intended safety control is unwired; not Critical because a genuinely empty/drained pool usually reverts the tx (gas-only loss) rather than draining the stake, and the stake is bounded by buyAmountSol. This is the prior audit's deferred 'on-chain pool verification before acting on migration' item — status: still_open.

title: peakLiquidityUsd is never seeded from on-chain reserves, so the pool-drain exit is blind to a pre-index rug
evidence: pos.peakLiquidityUsd is written in exactly one place — the monitor tick, from dexData.liquidityUsd (sniperEngine.ts:3763) — and only when dexData.hasPair && dexData.liquidityUsd>0. The position object created in executeBuy never seeds it (sniperEngine.ts:2931-2959 has no peakLiquidityUsd field), so at entry it is undefined. isPoolDrained is called with peakLiquidityUsd: pos.peakLiquidityUsd ?? 0 (3749) and requires peak >= minPeakUsd(2000), so the first observation can never fire, and if the first DexScreener reading arrives AFTER a rug the drained value becomes the recorded 'peak'. Pre-migration positions are covered separately by CURVE_DRAINED from on-chain curve reserves (3521-3535), so the exposure is specifically the post-migration / Play 3 path — the bot's main strategy per the code comments.

With no price stop-loss underneath (owner-intentional) the bag is held to zero — an uncapped loss on the strategy the bot runs most.
proposed_fix: Seed pos.peakLiquidityUsd at entry from the same on-chain reserve read proposed in finding #1 (2 * SOL-side reserve in USD), so the drain fraction is measured against real graduation depth from tick one rather than against whatever DexScreener happens to report first.
verdict_reason: Verified in the working tree. peakLiquidityUsd is written in exactly one place (sniperEngine.ts:3763, pos.peakLiquidityUsd = Math.max(pos.peakLiquidityUsd ?? 0, dexData.liquidityUsd)), gated behind dexData.hasPair && dexData.liquidityUsd>0 (3746). The position literal in executeBuy (2931-2959) contains no peakLiquidityUsd field, so at entry it is undefined; the drain check reads pos.peakLiquidityUsd ?? 0 (3749) and isPoolDrained (pipelineUtils.ts:386-389) short-circuits on `!(peakLiquidityUsd >= 2000)`. A grep across the tree shows NO seeding site — only the write at 3763, the reads at 3749/3753, the type at types.ts:456, and tests. Confirmed refute-attempts: (a) CURVE_DRAINED (sniperEngine.ts:2518-2535) reads on-chain curve reserves and applies only to on-curve/pre-migration positions — once migrated the curve stops updating, so it does NOT cover the post-migration DexScreener path; (b) the time stop (exitOnMaxHold, 3663-3669) and no-data exit (3652-3658) are backstops but do not restore the structural early-exit; (c) a fully-pulled pool (current=0) is unsellable regardless since isPoolDrained requires currentLiquidityUsd>0 (388) — but the real loss is the sellable partial-drain case: a token that indexes only AFTER a $12k->$5k pull records peak=$5k, so the original 58% drop never arms POOL_DRAINED and the owner-enabled structural exit silently fails to fire while liquidity is still sellable. This is a genuine missed exit on the primary post-migration play. Prior audits flag it as still_open (phaseCDE line 59 'Specified, not implemented'; phaseB attack 4 DIE-class). High stands.

title: A buy not confirmed within 30s opens a position on estimated tokens with no on-chain balance reconciliation
evidence: confirmTransaction polls getSignatureStatus for a fixed 30_000ms (sniperEngine.ts:1678-1704), which is shorter than a Solana blockhash's ~60-90s validity — so the confirm window closes while the tx's fate is still undecided. On a buy timeout executeRealMainnetTrade returns { txid, fill: null } (1624-1637). executeBuy sees result truthy but result.fill null, so it does NOT return; it registers a position with the pre-trade ESTIMATE tokensHeld = investedUsd/buyPriceUsd (2864) and fillVerified=false (2931-2962). The bad-fill guard is skipped because it requires fillVerified (2977). No code path ever reads the wallet's actual token balance to reconcile: there is no getTokenAccountsByOwner/getTokenAccountBalance anywhere in src/services (grep empty), and the constructor comment concedes 'nothing in this codebase reads an on-chain token balance' (458). inspectFill only works on a landed tx (fillInspector.ts:63-70).
impact: Under the RPC congestion that is normal while sniping, a buy that never lands (blockhash expiry / drop) creates a phantom position: it occupies a maxActivePositions slot, shows fabricated PnL, and burns exit-retry fees on every tick until the 20-attempt cap (sellPctReal 3287) before giving up. A buy that lands after second 30 becomes a real position carrying an estimated cost basis the bad-fill guard never vetted.
proposed_fix: On a buy timeout, do not open on estimates; either extend confirmation to the blockhash's actual last-valid-block-height (getSignatureStatuses / confirmTransaction with the fetched blockhash) or, after opening, verify tokensHeld against an on-chain getTokenAccountBalance for the mint before the position is treated as real, closing it out when the balance is zero.
verdict_reason: Verified end to end. confirmTransaction defaults to 30000ms (sniperEngine.ts:1678) polling getSignatureStatus, and on a buy timeout executeRealMainnetTrade returns { txid, fill: null } (1624-1637). In executeBuy, result is truthy so it does not return (2906); result.fill is null so the reconcile block (2916-2928) is skipped, leaving the pre-trade ESTIMATE tokensHeld = investedUsd/buyPriceUsd (2864) and fillVerified=false (2871,2945). The bad-fill guard requires fillVerified and is therefore skipped (2977). No on-chain token-balance reconciliation exists anywhere: grep for getTokenAccountsByOwner/getTokenAccountBalance/getParsedTokenAccounts in src is empty, the constructor concedes 'nothing in this codebase reads an on-chain token balance' (458), and inspectFill returns null unless the tx landed without error (fillInspector.ts:57-70) and is only invoked in the confirmed branch (1647), not on timeout. fillVerified is used only for display/guard/labeling (1135,2977,3192,3984,4011) — no path removes or corrects a phantom position. A never-landed buy thus creates a phantom position occupying a maxActivePositions slot with fabricated PnL that burns up to ~20 backed-off sell fees (cap at 3287-3296) before auto-exits stop. Medium is honest (the 'burns fees every tick' phrasing is slightly loose — retries are exponentially backed off — but the substance holds).

title: Runtime RPC failover is absent: a Helius outage mid-run leaves the bot unable to price or exit positions
evidence: The Connection is built once at boot (sniperEngine.ts:509) and rebuilt only on a key/config change (884-887, 963-968) — never in response to runtime failures. resolveRpcEndpoint picks a single endpoint by static priority and only ever falls back to SOLANA_RPC_FALLBACK_URL / public when there is NO key (rpcHealth.ts:300-319), so with a Helius key set the bot stays pinned to Helius even if it goes down. rpcHealth() is observational only — read in getStatus (1311) for display; nothing acts on consecutiveFailures/credentialRejected to switch endpoints. The engine's own hot-path calls (sendRawTransaction 1569, getSignatureStatus 1682, getAccountInfo in localTxBuilder) do not even go through withRpcRetry.
impact: During a Helius outage or sustained 429 storm, the monitor tick cannot fetch quotes and executeRealMainnetTrade cannot confirm sells, so OPEN positions (real money) cannot be priced or exited until an operator manually changes the key/URL and restarts. The bot appears alive while its live path is dead.
proposed_fix: On a run of consecutive hot-path RPC failures (rpcHealth already counts them), rebuild solanaConnection against SOLANA_RPC_FALLBACK_URL / public and rebind localTxBuilder, then probe the primary and switch back when it recovers.
verdict_reason: Verified: solanaConnection is built once at boot (sniperEngine.ts:509) and rebuilt only on a Helius key change (885, 964) — never in response to runtime failures. resolveRpcEndpoint returns the Helius URL whenever a key is present and only falls back to SOLANA_RPC_FALLBACK_URL/public when there is NO key (rpcHealth.ts:308-319), so with a key set the bot stays pinned to Helius through an outage. rpcHealth() is observational: read only in getStatus (1311) to populate the status payload (surfaced in App.tsx:783,820); nothing acts on consecutiveFailures/credentialRejected to switch endpoints. The exit hot path (sendRawTransaction 1569, getSignatureStatus 1682) bypasses withRpcRetry entirely, and withRpcRetry (used only in walletService/honeypotDetector) merely retries the same endpoint. The copy trader routes its real exits through this same connection via executeExternalTrade, so a Helius outage/429-storm blocks pricing and confirmation of real-money exits on the actively-trading path until an operator changes the key/URL and restarts. Matches the prior audit's deferred 'runtime RPC failover' item — still open. Medium is defensible: the impact is real and touches the live exit path, but it is contingent on an external provider outage, is recoverable by operator action, and the RPC-failure state is surfaced in the UI (not fully silent), which keeps it below the 'silently bricks while appearing alive' bar; it sits on the Medium/High boundary but Medium is honest.

title: The sniper's own timed-out sell can execute twice; the double-submit guard was applied only to external/copy callers
evidence: On a sell timeout executeRealMainnetTrade returns opts.external ? { txid, fill:null, timedOut:true } : null (sniperEngine.ts:1624-1631). The inline comment (1627-1630) explains that a timed-out percentage sell 'can still land until its blockhash expires, and a blind resubmit of a percentage sell executes twice', and hands external (copy-exit) callers the signature so they resolve the outcome first — but the sniper's own exits receive null. sellPctReal treats null as a hard failure: it increments sellFailCount, sets an exponential backoff, and returns null (3279-3298), after which the next monitor tick / take-profit rung re-invokes sellPctReal with a fresh `${pct}%` order. Partial rungs (3781, 3832, 3845, 3858, 3877) call sellPctReal directly and are not protected by pos.exitInFlight (only executeSell sets that, 3898).
impact: If the original (timed-out) sell lands within the blockhash's remaining validity and the resubmit also lands, the position is sold more than intended — an extra partial exit plus an extra priority+protocol fee, directly contrary to the owner's hold-biased policy. inspectFill keeps per-leg accounting correct, so this is an unintended trade rather than a PnL miscount.
proposed_fix: Give the sniper's own sell path the same treatment as the external path: on a sell timeout, return the signature and resolve its on-chain outcome (resolveTimedOutSell already exists at 698) before submitting any resubmit, rather than treating an unconfirmed sell as 'did not happen'.
verdict_reason: Verified. executeRealMainnetTrade signature (sniperEngine.ts:1437) defaults opts={}, and the sniper's own exit calls it without opts (sellPctReal, sniperEngine.ts:3278), so on a sell timeout the ternary at 1631 returns null for the internal path (the {txid,fill:null,timedOut:true} escape is external-only). sellPctReal treats null as a hard failure: sellFailCount++ and sellRetryAfterMs = now + 5_000 on the first miss (3280-3298), then returns null. The confirm timeout is 30s (confirmTransaction default timeoutMs=30000, 1678-1704) while a submitted tx stays landable until blockhash expiry ~60-90s (author's own comments at 65, 692, 1628) — so the timed-out sell can still land after the 5s backoff resubmit fires from the next tick, producing a duplicate partial exit. The partial rungs at 3781/3832/3845/3858/3877 call sellPctReal(pos,50) directly and never set pos.exitInFlight (only executeSell does, 3898-3899), and they don't set their rung flag when sale===null, so the rung re-triggers. Author explicitly acknowledges the double-execute risk (1627-1630) yet guarded only external callers. Medium is honest: bounded to one extra partial exit + one extra fee against a hold-biased policy, and inspectFill keeps per-leg accounting correct (1647-1652), so it's an unintended trade not a PnL miscount.

title: Clean shutdown is never recorded, so every restart with open positions falsely reports a crash (markCleanShutdown is dead code)
evidence: persistPositions(cleanShutdown=false) is the only writer and is always called with the default false (sniperEngine.ts:2962 and 3948); toggleBot(false) does not persist a clean marker (996-1114) and there is no process shutdown hook that does (server.ts has only uncaughtException/unhandledRejection at 49-50; realModeLock's SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers touch only the lock). positionStore.markCleanShutdown (positionStore.ts:210) is therefore never invoked. positionStore.load computes crashed = (parsed.cleanShutdown !== true) (positionStore.ts:202), so describeRestoration always emits 'the previous process did NOT exit cleanly' even after a deliberate stop.
impact: The crash-vs-clean signal the store was carefully built to provide is always 'crashed', crying wolf on every normal restart and eroding the one boot-time warning meant to flag genuinely orphaned bags. Positions are still restored and surfaced, so no funds are lost.
proposed_fix: Call positionStore.markCleanShutdown(snapshot, meta) from toggleBot(false) and from a real SIGINT/SIGTERM handler in the server, so a deliberate stop is distinguishable from a crash.
verdict_reason: Verified. persistPositions has cleanShutdown default false (sniperEngine.ts:3334) and both call sites pass nothing — after opening (2962) and after closing (3948) a position. toggleBot(false)'s else-branch (1095-1111) never persists a clean marker, and there is no runtime process-shutdown hook that calls markCleanShutdown. positionStore.markCleanShutdown (positionStore.ts:210) is invoked only from a test (src/tests/guardrailProofs.ts:220) — never in the runtime path, so the finding's substance holds despite the slight imprecision of 'never invoked'. load() computes crashed = parsed.cleanShutdown !== true (positionStore.ts:202), and describeRestoration prints 'the previous process did NOT exit cleanly' whenever crashed (228). It is wired at boot (sniperEngine.ts:463-465) and only fires when open positions exist (positionStore.ts:225), so every deliberate restart carrying a bag falsely reports a crash. Low is honest: positions are still restored, no funds lost.

title: migrationSeenAt map grows unbounded over a long run
evidence: this.migrationSeenAt.set(payload.mint, arrivalMs) runs on every migrate event off the websocket (sniperEngine.ts:1792) and is read at 2699, but the map is never pruned or deleted from (grep migrationSeenAt shows only the field decl at 432, the set at 1792, and the get at 2699 — no delete, no size cap, and it is not cleared in toggleBot). proposed_fix: Prune migrationSeenAt on the existing 60s watchlist prune interval (drop entries older than the Play 3 window), or evict an entry once its mint is opened/abandoned.
verdict_reason: Verified. Repo-wide grep shows exactly three references to migrationSeenAt: the field decl (sniperEngine.ts:432), the set on every 'migrate' event while the bot is active (1791-1792, inside the WS message handler after the isBotActive guard at 1782), and one get (2699). No delete, no size cap, no clear in toggleBot or anywhere. title: Auto-updater has no code-provenance verification and points at the divergent-lineage repo; one-click update replaces the wallet-holding binary with untrusted code
evidence: repoOwner/repoName are hardcoded to `jgouiza-debug`/`pumpfun-sniper-bot` (updaterService.ts:67-68) — the exact repo the task states now carries the DIVERGENT v1.0.9–v1.1.0 releases that lack this tree's fixes. checkForUpdates() fetches GitHub `/releases/latest` (updaterService.ts:172), and isVersionGreater('1.1.0','1.0.8') returns true via integer part-compare (updaterService.ts:267-279), so hasUpdate=true and App.tsx:341/355 surfaces an update banner (polled every 5 min). applyUpdate() then downloads the asset (updaterService.ts:393) and 'verifies' it against a SHA256 fetched from the SAME release's own assets (`${binAsset.name}.sha256`, updaterService.ts:209-211; fetched at :396, compared at :400-403). The checksum is self-referential: it proves only that the download matches what that release published, not that the publisher is trusted. There is NO code signing and NO pinned key anywhere in the module. The progress string 'Verifying signature…' (updaterService.ts:395) and the refusal comment 'refusing to install an unverified binary' (updaterService.ts:376) misrepresent a hash-equality check as cryptographic provenance.
impact: Benign case: a user clicking the update banner silently regresses their install onto the divergent lineage that is missing this tree's copy-trading gas fixes (v1.0.4–v1.0.8), because 1.1.0 compares greater than 1.0.8. Malicious case: a compromised GitHub account (or the divergent branch owner) publishes a release whose binary is a wallet-drainer; it passes the SHA256 'verification' because the attacker controls both the binary and its .sha256, then the swap-and-relaunch (updaterService.ts:428-439) runs the attacker's code beside `.photon-wallet.json` — full key/fund loss. TLS + checksum only defend the transit hop; neither defends provenance. Click-gated (window.confirm at App.tsx:368, token-gated POST, mid-trade refusal) rather than fully automatic, which is the only reason this is not a zero-interaction drainer.
proposed_fix: Add real provenance: ship a detached signature (minisign/cosign) over each binary and verify it in applyUpdate against a public key baked into the build, refusing on signature failure. Alternatively pin an allowlist of known-good release SHA256es compiled into the binary. Until the lineage is reconciled, disable self-update against jgouiza-debug/pumpfun-sniper-bot or require the user to confirm the exact repo+version+hash. Stop labeling the hash check 'Verifying signature'.
verdict_reason: All code-level facts confirmed: repoOwner='jgouiza-debug' (updaterService.ts:67-68); isVersionGreater does an integer part-compare so [1,1,0] beats [1,0,8] at index 1 -> hasUpdate true (267-279); the checksum is fetched from the SAME release's own assets (`${binAsset.name}.sha256`, 209-211) and compared by hash equality only (396-403); there is NO code signing or pinned key anywhere in the module (read in full); and the UI string 'Verifying signature…' (395) plus 'refusing to install an unverified binary' (376) misrepresent a transit-integrity hash as cryptographic provenance. However, Critical overstates it. The fund/key-loss outcome is NOT reachable by the bot's own operation, ordinary market data, or a network fault — it requires an EXTERNAL precondition (takeover of the GitHub release channel or a malicious publish) AND is gated behind three live-path controls I verified: a browser window.confirm (App.tsx:368), a token-authenticated POST via apiFetch (App.tsx:387; server.ts:488 'token-gated'), and a restart guard that refuses whenever any sniper/copy position is open or either engine is armed (server.ts:501-517). So it is neither an unconditional nor a silent ('while appearing alive') fund-loss/brick path — the Critical bar. The strongest defensible severity is High: a self-replacing wallet-holding binary with no code-provenance check, an auto-surfaced update banner (polled every 5 min, App.tsx:355) whose 'Verifying signature' copy actively induces false trust, PLUS a no-precondition benign regression — the version math installs any higher-numbered divergent release, reintroducing the copy-exit gas bug fixed in v1.0.4-v1.0.8 — which is a major reliability hole in the live path.

title: Real-mode double-spend lock is keyed on process.cwd(), not the install dir, so two instances launched with different working directories both acquire it
evidence: LOCK_FILE = path.resolve(process.cwd(), '.real-mode.lock') (realModeLock.ts:4). This mutex is the live fund-safety guard: sniperEngine.ts:1032-1043 calls realModeLock.acquire() before arming REAL mode and its comment claims 'One live instance at a time, machine-wide … two armed at once would double-spend the balance' (sniperEngine.ts:1029-1031). The atomic create-if-absent open('wx') (realModeLock.ts:100-107) only serializes instances that resolve to the SAME cwd path. By contrast apiAuth.ts:35-40 deliberately uses the exe directory (dirname(process.execPath)) when packaged 'so the instance switcher keeps working' — the lock does not follow that rule. Two copies of the same packaged exe signing with the same Photon wallet but launched with different cwds (double-click → cwd=install dir; a .bat with `cd`, a shortcut 'Start in', or Task Scheduler → a different cwd, e.g. System32) write to two different `.real-mode.lock` files and BOTH acquire successfully.
impact: The 'machine-wide' single-live-instance guarantee fails open under mixed-launch conditions: both instances read the same wallet balance, size against it independently, and issue duplicated buys — the exact double-spend / blown-gas-float the lock exists to prevent. Silent: each instance believes it holds an exclusive lock.
proposed_fix: Key the lock on a machine-global fixed path (e.g. os.tmpdir() or a well-known per-user app-data path) or, better, on the wallet address (the real shared resource), not process.cwd(). At minimum use the exe directory when packaged to match apiAuth's base-dir rule.
verdict_reason: The mechanism is real: LOCK_FILE = path.resolve(process.cwd(), '.real-mode.lock') (realModeLock.ts:4) and acquire's atomic open('wx') (100) only serialize instances that resolve to the same cwd path, unlike apiAuth.ts:35-40 which uses dirname(process.execPath) when packaged. But the finder's load-bearing premise — 'signing with the same Photon wallet but launched with different cwds' — is only conditionally true, and the miss narrows the severity. WALLET_FILE is ALSO cwd-resolved (walletService.ts:26, path.resolve(process.cwd(), '.photon-wallet.json')), and autoLoad's precedence (walletService.ts:172-198) is env PHOTON_PRIVATE_KEY first, then the cwd file. So under the DOCUMENTED primary configuration — the UI-linked key persisted to .photon-wallet.json, which clientWallet.ts:13 calls 'the only at-rest copy' — a second instance launched with a different cwd (e.g. System32) finds no .photon-wallet.json, loads no wallet, and cannot sign real trades, so it cannot double-spend; the cwd-scoped lock and cwd-scoped wallet are mutually consistent, and same-cwd launches (including instance-switcher child spawns that inherit cwd) share the SAME lock file and serialize correctly. The double-spend materializes ONLY when the key is supplied via the exe-dir .env (PHOTON_PRIVATE_KEY), which IS shared across cwds while the lock is not, AND two instances are launched with different cwds AND both armed to REAL on that shared wallet. That is a genuine but bounded, configuration-and-launch-dependent gap in the fund-safety lock (the invariant asserted at sniperEngine.ts:1029-1030), not a broad live-path reliability failure — Medium per 'real but bounded operational impact,' not High.

title: Window-close and /api/server/shutdown exit paths bypass the mid-trade guard the updater enforces, abandoning open positions and in-flight txs
evidence: The app-window child 'exit' handler calls sniperEngine.toggleBot(false) then server.close(...=>process.exit(0)) plus a 3s unconditional setTimeout(()=>process.exit(0)) (server.ts:702-708) with no open-position / in-flight-tx check. /api/server/shutdown likewise does process.exit(0) after 500ms with no guard (server.ts:324-330). This is asymmetric with the update path, whose restartGuard explicitly refuses to exit while ANY sniper position, copy position, or active bot exists (server.ts:501-517, enforced in updaterService.ts:360-363 and re-checked at :406-407) precisely because 'restarting with an open position would strand it between processes'.
impact: Closing the desktop app window (the documented 'close = stop' gesture) during an open REAL position halts all exit monitoring for that bag, and the 3-second hard process.exit can kill a buy/sell that is mid-submission. The updater treats this exact state as unsafe and refuses; the window/shutdown paths do it unconditionally. Positions are not persisted (prior audit §1.5), so an in-memory bag is simply lost on exit. The shutdown intent itself is owner-intended; the defensible gap is the unguarded abandonment of open positions / in-flight txs.
proposed_fix: Reuse the updater's restartGuard on the window-close and /api/server/shutdown paths: warn (or block, or force-flush/await in-flight sells) when positions are open or a tx is in flight, instead of an immediate process.exit. At minimum log the stranded positions before exiting so the durable bot.log records what was abandoned.
verdict_reason: The cited code is accurate: the window 'exit' handler calls toggleBot(false) then server.close(->exit) plus an unconditional setTimeout(->exit,3000) with no open-position/in-flight check (server.ts:702-708), /api/server/shutdown exits after 500ms with no guard (324-330), and the updater's restartGuard does refuse to exit while any sniper position, copy position, or active bot exists (501-517). But the Medium rests on a stale/false premise. The finding states 'Positions are not persisted (prior audit §1.5), so an in-memory bag is simply lost on exit' — in the current tree positions ARE persisted on every mutation (persistPositions at sniperEngine.ts:2962 on open, 3948 on close) and restored+reconciled at boot (positionStore.load at 463, describeRestoration marks them UNRECONCILED). So the bag is not lost; it survives the stop. Moreover 'stop = pause entries, RETAIN open positions' is the owner's intended model (/api/bot/kill comment server.ts:318; toggleBot(false) never liquidates, 1095-1111), and the updater's guard exists for a different hazard it doesn't share — a NEW process racing for the real-mode lock held by a vanishing PID ('stranded between two processes', 496-498). The only residual novel gap is the 3s hard process.exit possibly truncating a tx still being built (an already-broadcast tx lands regardless, and state reconciles on next boot) plus the absence of an open-position warning on close. That is bounded to Low, not Medium.

title: Run reports are written to process.cwd()/reports instead of the exe directory, scattering or failing when launched with a foreign cwd
evidence: REPORTS_DIR = path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'reports') (reportService.ts:5), used by persist() (reportService.ts:277-279) and listSavedReports() (reportService.ts:260-269). Both fileLogger.ts:21-22 and apiAuth.ts:37-39 branch to dirname(process.execPath) when packaged specifically because 'a Task Scheduler launch has cwd C:\Windows\System32, and a log written there is a log nobody finds' (fileLogger.ts comment). reportService does not apply that rule.

Bounded: reports are diagnostic and the write error is caught (reportService.ts:281-283).
proposed_fix: Compute REPORTS_DIR with the same isPackaged ? dirname(process.execPath) : process.cwd() base-dir helper used by fileLogger/apiAuth, ideally factored into one shared function.
verdict_reason: Verified. reportService.ts:5 sets REPORTS_DIR = path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'reports') unconditionally, and it is used by persist (mkdir+writeFileSync at 277-279) and listSavedReports (260-269). By contrast fileLogger.ts:21-22 and apiAuth.ts:37-39 both branch to path.dirname(process.execPath) when isPackaged, with fileLogger's comment naming the exact hazard (a Task Scheduler launch has cwd C:\Windows\System32). reportService does not apply that rule, so a packaged exe launched with a foreign cwd writes reports under that cwd (e.g. System32\reports) while bot.log and .api-token correctly land beside the exe. The bot is shipped as an exe (dist-exe present) and Task-Scheduler launches are a documented scenario, so the path is reachable.
